report.tagline: The swipe-based dating app owned by Match Group, now trying to win back Gen Z after years of shrinking users.
report.simpleSummary: Tinder shows you photos of people nearby, one at a time. Swipe right if you like them, left if you don't, and if both of you swipe right it's a 'match' and you can chat. It is free to use, but you can pay for extras like seeing who already liked you or unlimited swipes. Tinder made swiping famous, but many young people now find it tiring, so it is adding new ways to meet, like going on a double date with a friend.

overview.whatItDoes: Tinder helps people meet new people nearby for dates, relationships or friendship. You build a profile with photos and a short bio, swipe through others, and chat only when both people like each other. Match Group, which also owns Hinge, makes money by selling subscriptions and one-off boosts.
howItWorks: Sign up with a phone number, add photos, age, interests and what you are looking for.
Tinder shows a stack of nearby profiles ranked by its algorithm.
Swipe right to like, left to pass, or send a Super Like to stand out.
When two people like each other, they match and can message.
Free users get limited likes; paid plans (Tinder Plus, Gold and Platinum) add unlimited likes, see who liked you, and priority.
Safety tools like Face Check (a video selfie check) and photo verification fight fake profiles.
overview.valueProposition: The biggest pool of single people in most cities, with a fast and simple way to find a match, free to start.

businessModel.summary: Tinder makes money mainly from subscriptions (Plus, Gold, Platinum) and one-off purchases like Boosts and Super Likes. There are also some ads. Revenue depends on the number of payers times what each pays.

revenueStreams.detail: Tinder Plus, Gold and Platinum. Most of revenue. Prices vary by country, age and plan length.
Boosts, Super Likes and other one-off items.
Ads shown between profiles to free users; a small share of revenue.

businessModel.pricing: Free to start. In the US, Tinder Gold often costs about $25 to $40 a month depending on age and plan length; Platinum costs more. In India, monthly plans are usually a few hundred to over ₹1,000. Prices are personalised and not published as a single list.
costDrivers: App store fees of up to 30% on in-app purchases; Match warned of higher fees from 2027
Marketing to win back users, especially Gen Z
Trust and safety teams and verification tools
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take one US Gold subscriber paying about $30 a month. Apple or Google may keep up to $9 in fees. The cost to run the app for that user is small, maybe $1 to $2. So Tinder keeps about $19 a month, or about $230 a year if the user stays. Most users never pay, so Tinder needs a big free pool to keep paying users matching. Key ratio: payers divided by monthly users. If users fall, payers fall too, which is why Tinder's revenue dropped even as prices rose.

howTheyGetUsers: Brand fame: 'Tinder' is the word many people use for dating apps
Word of mouth from friends who met partners
Performance marketing and campus campaigns aimed at Gen Z
Features like Double Date that invite friends into the app
growth.moat: Tinder has the largest pool of users in most cities. Daters go where the most people are, so a new app struggles to compete. This network effect weakens if Gen Z stops using dating apps altogether.

competitors.name: Hinge
competitors.positioning: 'Designed to be deleted', focused on serious relationships with prompts.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tinder is faster and more casual. Hinge, also owned by Match, is growing about 19% a year while Tinder shrinks.

competitors.name: Bumble
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tinder has a bigger user base; Bumble is shrinking and agreed in 2026 to be taken private.

competitors.name: Aisle and other Indian apps
competitors.positioning: Serious relationships for Indians, often with paid messaging.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tinder is more casual and urban; Aisle targets marriage-minded users.

competitors.name: Instagram and in-person events
competitors.positioning: Meeting through social media, friends and run clubs.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tinder offers a direct path to new single people, but many Gen Z users prefer meeting 'organically'.

northStar.metric: Weekly number of mutual conversations that lead to an exchange of at least 10 messages or a date
northStar.why: Tinder's value is real connections, not swipes. Good conversations are the closest measurable signal that users are meeting people they like.

pmLessons: A simple core action, like a swipe, can build a huge brand, but it can also start to feel shallow.
In a two-sided product, losing one side, like women users, hurts everyone.
Raising prices can hide user decline for a while, but revenue follows users over time.
Owning a rival (Hinge) can help the parent company even if the original brand shrinks.

interviewQuestions.question: Tinder monthly users are falling. How would you find out why?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment by age, gender and country. Look at sign-up, match and reply rates. Compare against Hinge and Bumble. List hypotheses and data to test.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to win back Gen Z users.
interviewQuestions.hint: Start with Gen Z needs (safety, groups, shared interests), propose one feature, define success metrics and a guardrail.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Tinder charge different prices by age?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh revenue against fairness and legal risk. Consider willingness to pay. Suggest test design and metrics.

interviewQuestions.question: What should Tinder's north star metric be?
interviewQuestions.hint: Choose meaningful conversations, not swipes. Break into active daters, match rate, conversation quality, safety.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase the share of women on Tinder?
interviewQuestions.hint: Identify why women leave (safety, low-effort messages), propose features, track women's retention.
